Credentials should never be stored in plain text but hashed before storage, because a hash is not reversible (so even staff cannot recover user passwords), is efficient to compute, and has near-zero collision probability so two passwords are extremely unlikely to share a hash.

A password-hashing algorithm should be slow on modern hardware to reduce the number of guesses per second an attacker can make, so a slow algorithm like BCrypt (which becomes slower as hardware gets faster) or PBKDF2 (which uses key stretching) is preferred; on breach, plaintext passwords are fully compromised, MD5 hashes are crackable with rainbow tables, and BCrypt hashes are unlikely to be cracked.

Offering two-factor authentication eliminates remote logins not initiated by the account owner in the absence of vulnerabilities in the 2FA app or protocol, since compromise then requires both the password and the physical device; a hardware USB token is more secure than phone or SMS 2FA, which is still an order of magnitude safer than no 2FA.
condition: in the absence of vulnerabilities in the 2FA app or messaging protocol

statement: When storing personally identifiable information or financial data, ensure the storage is legal and compliant with the laws of every country of operation and that a breach would not expose the data in an easily abusable format; a smaller company may find it more effective to outsource storage of such data to a compliant specialist.

A custom search engine usually requires a separate database from the primary one because search data must be stored for efficient querying, and syncing the two introduces security risks such as permission-model drift, objects deleted in the primary but not the search database, and stale metadata that remains searchable after removal, so the architecture must be planned up front.

Architecture-phase security flaws are far more costly to fix later because customers may rely on the insecure functionality and need a migration plan, deep flaws can require rewriting many dependent modules and even swapping an underlying technology, the flaw may already have been exploited at real financial cost, and it may be published, bringing bad PR and lost customers.

Code review must always occur after the architecture review and never before, because a move-fast-and-break-things philosophy is often abused to skip security; at minimum the major, well-known features should be architected and reviewed, and each new feature architected and reviewed for security before development.

Organizations that perform only functional code reviews should add a code security review as an additional step, ideally at merge-request time when the full feature is integrated, because an additional reviewer from outside the immediate development team provides unbiased eyes that catch otherwise-unknown bugs and architecture flaws; per-commit or pair-programming review suits mission-critical security features.

A code security review checks for common archetypes such as XSS, CSRF, and injection, but more importantly for logic-level vulnerabilities that require deep context into the feature's purpose and cannot be found by automated tools or scanners, which is why the reviewer must understand the feature's users, functionality, and business impact.

A custom logic vulnerability example is an API endpoint that trusts a client-supplied flag such as isMember:true and grants member-only functionality the user was never granted by a moderator, a privilege escalation that no generic vulnerability scanner would catch.

An effective security-review traversal starts at the client-side code to learn the business logic and user-facing surface area, follows the client's API calls to the server, traces the dependencies those APIs rely on (databases, logs, helper and conversion libraries), then looks for public APIs that are unintentionally exposed or intended for future features, and finally covers the rest of the codebase in descending order of risk.

Temporary or incomplete security mitigations should generally be avoided in favor of a permanent solution even if it takes longer, and a temporary solution should only be implemented when there is a preplanned timeline for designing and implementing the complete one.

Blacklists are a security anti-pattern because they only protect an application given perfect knowledge of all current and future malicious inputs, which is unattainable, so they can usually be bypassed with little effort (such as buying a new domain); whitelists are always preferable in security.

The maintenance burden of a whitelist can be reduced by combining manual and automated effort, for example requiring integrating partners to submit their website and business license for review before being whitelisted, which makes a malicious integration extremely difficult to slip through.

Default or boilerplate framework code is a security anti-pattern because frameworks too often ship insecure-by-default and require effort to tighten; default configs can leak information (such as a Rails 404 page revealing the version) or be dangerous (older MongoDB was internet-accessible with no authentication by default, leading to mass ransom hijacking), so boilerplate should never be launched to production without being evaluated and configured.

The trust-by-default anti-pattern is avoided by applying least privilege per module: rather than running an entire application under one user account holding logging, database, and disk permissions, each module should run under its own user with only the permissions that function requires, so a vulnerability in one module (such as the SQL module) does not give access to files or logs handled by the others.

The client/server coupling anti-pattern is avoided by developing the client and server independently and having them communicate over a predefined data format and network protocol, so a separated server can reject all HTML and accept only predefined authentication payloads, giving each module fewer and simpler security mechanisms than a monolith that must guard against many languages and data formats.

Applications with the best architecture experience the fewest and lowest-risk vulnerabilities, and those with sufficient code-review processes fewer than those without, but even securely architected and reviewed applications still need vulnerability-discovery processes that target production code rather than preproduction code.

Automating vulnerability discovery is essential because automation is cheap, effective, and long-lasting at finding routine flaws that slip past architects and reviewers, but it is not good at finding logical vulnerabilities specific to your application or vulnerabilities that require chaining several weak ones; its common forms are static analysis, dynamic analysis, and vulnerability regression testing.

Static analysis evaluates source code without executing it (as a linter or on each commit), should be configured for the OWASP top 10, can detect patterns such as innerHTML DOM manipulation, URL-param variables, dangerous DOM sinks, user strings used in queries, and state-changing GET requests, and can enforce best practices like rejecting endpoints missing authorization imports, but it is weak on dynamically typed languages and produces many false positives.

Dynamic analysis examines code after execution against a model of vulnerabilities, so it finds actual rather than merely potential vulnerabilities, handles dynamically typed languages well, and detects side-effect issues such as sensitive data left in memory or side-channel attacks, at the cost of being slower, requiring a production-like environment, and having higher maintenance and cost but fewer false positives than static analysis.

A vulnerability regression test can use any testing framework capable of reproducing the vulnerability — what distinguishes it from a functional test is its purpose, not its framework — and these tests should be run on commit or push hooks that reject the change on failure (with scheduled daily runs as a second-best choice), preventing already-closed vulnerabilities from re-entering the codebase.

An organization should publish a responsible disclosure program defining legally safe ways for users to test the application's security, a clear submission method and template, and a non-disclosure window, because internal testing will not cover all customer use cases and, since the law poorly distinguishes white-hat research from black-hat exploitation, tech-savvy users will not report vulnerabilities without an explicit safe path.

A bug bounty program adds a cash incentive beyond responsible disclosure to actively test an application and report vulnerabilities, and platforms such as HackerOne and BugCrowd lower the setup cost by providing legal templates and a submission and triage interface, so the two should be used together.

Third-party penetration testing firms differ from bug bounty hunters in that they can be assigned specific parts of an application and, through legal agreements, be safely provided with company source code for more accurate results; contracted tests should ideally target high-risk and newly written areas before release, with post-release tests valuable for high-risk areas and for confirming security mechanisms hold across platforms.

The first step in managing a reported vulnerability is reproducing it in a production-like environment, which confirms it is a real vulnerability rather than a user configuration error, avoids wasting engineering hours or paying a bounty on a false positive, and gives insight into the root cause needed to resolve it.

A staging environment for reproducing vulnerabilities should mimic production as closely as possible, have a fully automated setup, and contain mock users and objects rather than real customers, and pre-release features should only be available on a build accessible via the internal network or secured by an encrypted login.

The Common Vulnerability Scoring System is a freely published, general-purpose system that ranks vulnerabilities by how easy they are to exploit and what data or processes can be compromised, making it a good starting point for organizations with limited budgets, though it is criticized for not accurately scoring rare, unique, or chained vulnerabilities.

CVSS produces a base score (the vulnerability in a vacuum, from eight inputs: attack vector, attack complexity, privileges required, user interaction, scope, and confidentiality/integrity/availability impact), a temporal score (mitigation maturity and report quality over time), and an environmental score (the vulnerability relative to your application's requirements), yielding a 0-to-10 number mapped to low, medium, high, and critical severity bands.

An organization can develop its own vulnerability scoring system starting from CVSS to capture business- and architecture-specific risk, which is especially advisable for applications that interface with physical or IoT technology (such as a web-controlled security camera that could leak footage), and any scoring system should be evaluated over time by its ability to prevent damage.

Vulnerability severity scoring can be used to prioritize fixes but must not be the only metric; other business-centric metrics such as customer contracts and business relationships must also be considered.

Vulnerabilities should be resolved with permanent, application-wide solutions whenever possible; when that is not yet possible, a temporary fix should be deployed and a new bug opened detailing the still-vulnerable surface area, and a bug should never be closed on a partial fix without first opening a follow-up bug, because closing early loses reproduction knowledge, not all vulnerabilities are reported, and risk grows as the application's surface area increases.

Every closed security bug should ship with a regression test, because regression tests grow increasingly valuable over time as the opportunities for regression increase exponentially with the size and feature set of a codebase.

The major rule for preventing XSS is to never allow unsanitized user-supplied data to be passed into the DOM; allowing user data into the DOM should be a last-resort fallback, and when required the data should be passed as a string that is interpreted as text rather than as DOM.

When appending true strings or string-like objects to the DOM, innerText should be preferred over innerHTML because innerText performs its own sanitization that renders HTML tags as strings while innerHTML interprets them as DOM, though innerText is not failsafe because each browser implements it differently and bypasses exist.

Complete sanitization is extremely hard: even a sanitizer that blocks single and double quotes and script tags can be bypassed by the JavaScript pseudo-scheme (a javascript: URL in an href) which executes without script tags or quotes, and by deriving blocked strings with String.fromCharCode, so the javascript: URL scheme should always be avoided.

A good rule of thumb is that any DOM API that converts text to DOM or text to script is a potential XSS sink, so the following should be avoided when possible: innerHTML, outerHTML, Blob, SVG, document.write, document.writeln, DOMParser.parseFromString, and document.implementation.

SVG and Blob are especially dangerous XSS sinks: an SVG relies on the XML spec that permits script execution and can run JavaScript on load (more dangerous than an img tag), and a Blob is a container for arbitrary data including base64 that is capable of code execution, so blobs should be left out of code whenever possible, especially when their instantiation involves user data.

Manually creating DOM nodes with document.createElement and organizing them with document.appendChild is significantly safer than DOMParser.parseFromString, because you then control the structure and tag names of the DOM while a user payload only controls the content.

User-supplied links can be sanitized by leveraging the browser's well-tested built-in anchor-tag sanitization (assigning the value to a dummy a element's href and reading it back, which also restricts the URL scheme) and by using encodeURIComponent for URL components, since these standard encoders are far safer than a home-brewed solution; encodeURIComponent must not be applied to an entire URL because it would corrupt the scheme and origin.
Performing HTML entity encoding on all HTML tags in user-supplied data lets the characters be displayed in the browser while preventing them from being interpreted as JavaScript.

HTML entity encoding of the big-five characters (&, <, >, double quote, single quote) lets user-supplied characters display in the browser without being interpreted as JavaScript, but it only protects content injected into a div-like DOM node and does NOT protect content injected inside a script tag, CSS, or a URL.

CSS is not a display-only technology but an attack vector: a user-uploaded stylesheet can leak data because the background:url attribute issues an HTTP GET (with query params) to any domain, and conditional selectors can change that background based on a form field's state to exfiltrate the form data to a hacker's server.

Because CSS is much harder to sanitize than JavaScript, CSS attacks are best prevented by, in increasing order of difficulty, disallowing user-uploaded CSS, allowing only specific user-modifiable fields and generating the stylesheet on the server, or sanitizing any HTTP-initiating CSS attributes such as background:url.

Content Security Policy is a browser-enforced configuration that controls what external scripts can load, from where, and which DOM APIs may execute them; whitelisting script sources with script-src ('self' plus trusted origins) causes the browser to throw a violation and block a script from any unlisted source such as an attacker's domain, and because it is browser-enforced it is difficult to bypass.
Wildcard host whitelists in a CSP carry inherent risk, because whitelisting a pattern like *.example.com can become harmful if a future subdomain is repurposed to allow user-uploaded scripts.

When CSP is enabled, inline script execution and eval-like string-to-code interpretation are disabled by default and should not be re-enabled with unsafe-inline or unsafe-eval; instead, functions that interpret a string should be rewritten to pass a function rather than a string (for example to setTimeout), because any function interpreted as a string risks escape leading to code execution.

A CSP is implemented either by sending a Content-Security-Policy header with each response or by embedding a meta tag in the HTML, and it is wise to enact CSP as a first step in XSS mitigation when you already know which programming constructs and APIs your application will rely on, since the policy can be changed later.

XSS can be mitigated at the network, database, or client level, but the client is almost always the ideal mitigation point because an XSS requires client-side execution; applications should use a centralized function for appending to the DOM so sanitization is routine, and although a CSP is a great first measure it will not protect against DOM XSS, so many mitigations should be combined.

A first line of CSRF defense is verifying the origin and referer headers against a list of trusted origins, because these headers cannot be set programmatically with JavaScript in major browsers and so have a low chance of being spoofed; the origin header is sent on POST (and on HTTPS) while referer is sent on all requests unless rel=noreferrer is set, and a request with neither header present should be rejected.

Header verification alone fails when an attacker obtains an XSS on a whitelisted origin (so the forged request appears to come legitimately from your own servers), which is especially worrisome when the site hosts user-generated content, so header verification should be only a starting point and multiple forms of CSRF defense should be employed.

The most powerful and most commonly used CSRF defense is the anti-CSRF token: the server issues a cryptographically generated low-collision token (regenerated per session or per request) that the client returns on every form and AJAX request and the server verifies as live, authentic, and unmanipulated, forcing a cross-origin attacker to obtain a live token and target a specific user, with token expiration often killing the token before the victim acts.

A stateless API should not be made stateful just to add CSRF tokens; instead a stateless CSRF token should be built from a unique user identifier, a timestamp for expiration, and a cryptographic nonce whose key exists only on the server, which is practical and consumes fewer server resources than session management.

HTTP GET requests should never store or modify server-side state, because GET is the most common and most easily distributable CSRF vector via links and images, so reads should be split into GET requests and stateful writes into POST requests.

CSRF defenses are effective only when applied application-wide, so anti-CSRF middleware that validates the origin/referer headers and the CSRF token should run on every request before any route logic and reject failures up front, and the token automation should be replicated on the client by wrapping or proxying XMLHttpRequest to always inject the token.

XXE is easy to defend against by disabling external entities in the XML parser, typically a single configuration line, but because OWASP notes Java-based parsers are especially dangerous (many have XXE enabled by default), you should always check the parser's API documentation rather than assuming external entities are disabled by default.

Re-architecting an application to use JSON instead of XML can eliminate XXE risk where the payload is just lightweight hierarchical data, because XML's security risk stems from the power of its specification to incorporate external files and multimedia, making it inherently less secure than JSON's string-based key/value pairs, though XML remains preferable where the payload will be rendered or requires rigid schema validation.

XXE is a gateway attack that often starts as read-only but provides a recon platform to access data otherwise unreachable outside the web server, so its final impact can escalate from read-only data access to remote code execution and full server takeover.

SQL injection is both the most common form of injection and one of the easiest to defend against, and because the attack takes place in the SQL interpreter it is simple to detect, so with proper detection and mitigation the odds of exposure are quite low.

To find SQL injection risk in a codebase, compile a single list of all SQL implementations and domain-specific languages the application uses (applications often use more than one database), and search the server side with generic queries that span multiple SQL dialects, since persistent cross-session data lives only in server memory, disk/logs, or a database.

Prepared statements are the first-line defense against SQL injection: the query is compiled first with placeholder bind variables so its intent is fixed before any user-submitted data is presented, meaning a SELECT cannot be escaped into a DELETE or have another query appended; they are supported by almost every major SQL database and their only real trade-off is a usually minimal performance cost.

Database-specific string sanitizers that escape risky characters (such as Oracle's ESAPI encoder, MySQL's QUOTE, and mysql_real_escape_string) should always be used for a query that cannot be parameterized, but they are a mitigation rather than a comprehensive defense against SQL injection.
condition: when a query cannot be parameterized

statement: Secure-by-default coding should be applied to all injection targets, not just SQL; the highest-risk injection targets are task schedulers, compression/optimization libraries, remote backup scripts, databases, loggers, any call to the host OS, and any interpreter or compiler, and dependencies add risk because they pull in their own subdependencies that may fall into these categories.

The principle of least authority states that each module in a software system should only have access to the data and functionality required for it to operate, and it becomes more important as an application scales, because a compromised least-authority component (such as a backup CLI) cannot compromise the rest of the application, whereas a component running as admin could expose the entire server during an injection attack.

The biggest injection risk is functionality where the client sends commands to the server to be executed, a bad architectural practice that should be avoided at all costs, because a security-first application never allows a client to provide a query or command that will be executed on the server.

When user input must be fed into a server-side CLI or operation, always use a whitelist rather than a blacklist of allowed commands together with a well-defined acceptable syntax (order, frequency, parameters), because blacklists are a security risk: a newly added command could grant the user unwanted functionality.

A first measure against DoS attacks is building comprehensive server logging that records all requests alongside their response time, and manually logging the performance of asynchronous background job functions (such as a backup that runs without returning a response), so that accidental or malicious DoS attempts arriving through legitimate channels can be found.

Regex DoS is best defended by a code review process plus a static analysis tool or linter that scans regular expressions for evil greedy-backtracking patterns (such as a repeated group followed by +) and keeps them out of the codebase, and by ensuring no user-supplied regular expressions are used anywhere and that integrated applications do not use user-supplied or poorly written regex.

Unlike XSS, which is binary, DoS risk should be evaluated on a scale (such as high/medium/low) because it depends on resource consumption that is hard to categorize and on the victim's device — a function an attacker cannot easily exploit on a powerful desktop may be exploitable on an older mobile device — so one should err on the side of caution and treat all but the extremely-hard-to-exploit code as vulnerable.

DDoS attacks cannot be prevented, only mitigated, and usually overwhelm a target with a sheer volume of legitimate-looking traffic rather than exploiting a logic bug, using a botnet of malware-compromised devices that includes not only PCs but also mobile and IoT devices, which are often easier to compromise.

The easiest DDoS defense is a bandwidth management service that inspects each packet and drops those matching a malicious pattern (absorbing request volumes your own infrastructure cannot), supplemented by blackholing that routes suspicious or repeated traffic to a non-operating server (effective for small but not large attacks); because oversensitive filters also block legitimate traffic, deep metrics on legitimate users' usage patterns should be gathered before deploying aggressive mitigation.
Anti-DoS mitigations should be implemented once affordable even if you do not expect your application to be a target, in case it becomes one in the future.

A dependency tree comprises third-party dependencies, their dependencies (fourth-party), and deeper levels; manual code-level review of such a tree does not scale and is often impossible once fourth-party dependencies have their own dependencies, and a command like npm ls can list the entire tree for evaluation.

Each unique dependency and each unique version of each dependency must be evaluated, because one version may carry critical vulnerabilities that a later version does not, and components rarely standardize on the same version across the chain, so a large application with a hundred third-party dependencies can yield a tree of thousands or tens of thousands of unique subdependencies and versions.

Dependency trees should be evaluated by automation: model the tree as a data structure, evaluate every newly added dependency and its subtrees automatically, and compare the tree against a well-known, long-lived CVE database such as the NIST NVD (using a scanner like Snyk or a script over npm list --depth) to find known vulnerabilities.

A secure way to integrate a third-party dependency is to run it on its own server (ideally maintained by your organization) and communicate with it over HTTP using JSON payloads, which prevents script execution on the application server without vulnerability chaining and lets the dependency behave like a pure function if no state is persisted on it, at the cost of reduced performance and the caveat that confidential data sent there could still be exposed if the package is compromised.

The isolation concept can also be applied within a single server by giving modules hardware-defined process and memory boundaries, so that a risky package struggles to reach the resources and functionality of the main application.

Risk from package-manager dependencies can be reduced by auditing a specific dependency version and then locking the semantic version (major.minor.patch) to it, because most package managers auto-upgrade to the latest patch by default (npm prefixes a caret), and removing the caret pins the exact version instead.

Version-locking a dependency does not protect against a maintainer redeploying new code under an existing version number (honoring new-code-to-new-version is up to the maintainer in npm and several package managers), and it only pins the top-level dependency, not its descendant dependencies.

Running npm shrinkwrap pins the exact version of every dependency and subdependency in the tree, eliminating the risk of a dependency auto-updating to a vulnerable latest patch; to additionally eliminate the rare risk of a maintainer reusing a version number, the shrinkwrap file should reference Git SHAs or the organization should deploy its own package mirror with the correct versions.

Any third-party integration should be assumed to carry at least some expected security risk in exchange for reduced development time, a risk that cannot be eliminated but can be mitigated through isolation, independent evaluation of each specific version, version-locking, shrinkwrapping, and referencing Git SHAs or a private mirror.

An application's security architecture can serve as a proxy for the overall quality of its code, and this is a signal that hackers take very seriously when deciding which application to focus their efforts on.

Because modern hackers target logical vulnerabilities in application source code, collaboration between software developers and security experts has become essential and individual contribution is no longer as valuable as it was in the past.

CSRF attacks are mitigated by introducing additional rules for state-changing requests that the browser cannot automatically confirm, including eliminating state-changing GET requests, implementing CSRF tokens, and requiring 2FA confirmation on elevated API requests.

Single-attacker DoS is mitigated by scanning regular expressions for backtracking problems, preventing user API calls from reaching functions that consume significant server resources, and adding rate limitations to those functions when required.
DDoS mitigations should start at the firewall and work their way up, using techniques such as blackholing traffic and enlisting a bandwidth management service that specializes in DDoS.
